title: The business of the sommelier
lead: The Advanced Business of the Sommelier exam: costing wine, cocktails and flights, reading inventory sheets and running audits, building and correcting a list, buying, storing and equipment, and training the team.

intro.title: THE MATH THAT RUNS A PROGRAM
intro.text: Business of the Sommelier opens the Practical: a 50-minute written exam with a calculator. These four formulas carry most of it. Every number in this chapter is our own example.

lines.label: The exam
lines.text: 50 minutes, calculator provided, no negative points, short answers only. Time calls come at half time, ten minutes and two minutes.

lines.label: The method
lines.text: Turn every ingredient into a cost per ounce, multiply by the ounces poured, add them up, then divide by your target cost %.

know: From Level 2: list price = bottle cost ÷ target cost %.
Cost per ounce = container cost ÷ ounces in it; the Court's formulas use 25 oz for a 750 ml bottle.
A cocktail's cost is the sum of each ingredient's cost per ounce × ounces used.
A flight's cost is each wine's cost per ounce × its pour, added together.
A quarter barrel keg holds 29.3 liters, 992 oz.

lines.label: Usage
lines.text: Usage = beginning inventory + purchases - ending inventory. It's what actually left the shelf.

lines.label: Sold
lines.text: Cost of product sold = each item's pour cost × the pours your POS says you sold. The gap between the two is variance.

know: Variance = cost of product sold - usage; % variance = variance ÷ usage.
A negative variance means product left without being sold: miscounts, overpouring or theft.
Count open bottles in tenths, in the same direction every time, with the bar closed.
Lay the sheet out in the same order the bottles sit on the shelf.
Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ average inventory value; days in inventory = days in the period ÷ turnover.

facts.fact: Business of the Sommelier is the first part of the Practical: a timed 50-minute exam; time markers 'Half Time', 'Ten Minutes', 'Two Minutes', 'Pens Down'; answer sheet, inventory sheet, beverage list and beverage list correction sheet provided with a calculator, tasting mat, water, spit cup and dump bucket; no negative points; none of the questions require long answers; the beverage list has lots of mistakes, big and small.

Business of the Sommelier covers program management: qualitative assessment for pricing, theme and style; marketing and sales techniques; purchasing; costing; audits; list management; inventory management; staff management and training; beverage equipment management. Exercises include tasting and evaluating beverage alcohol, costing wine, cocktails and flights, reading and evaluating inventory sheets, and correcting mistakes on a beverage list.
Costing math is not on the Theory exam; it is in the Business of the Sommelier exam.

Expected skill set: complete beverage program management: list content, design and basic marketing; cellar design, purchasing and inventory systems; staff training for a single unit and mentorship toward Introductory or Certified; financial management with cost controls and spreadsheet creation/comprehension.

Curriculum Guide (Certified): Cost % = bottle cost ÷ list price; list price = bottle cost ÷ target cost %; BTG = (bottle list price ÷ 25 oz) × pour; pour cost starting from case cost; bottles needed = (guests × oz per guest) ÷ 25.
Curriculum Guide (Beer, Certified): FIFO for restocking; a Quarter Barrel keg = 29.3 liters / 992 ounces; one pint = 16 ounces.

Cost per ounce = container cost ÷ ounces per container; liquor cost % = COGS ÷ alcohol sales; inventory turnover = COGS ÷ average inventory value; average days in inventory = days in period ÷ inventory turnover.
Markup = (sale price - cost) ÷ cost; profit margin = profit ÷ sale price.
By-the-glass and flight pricing: calculate the cost per ounce or pour and apply a markup.

Usage = starting inventory + received inventory - ending inventory. Cost of product sold = pour cost × pours sold, using the POS product mix (PMIX). $ variance = cost of product sold - usage; % variance = $ variance ÷ usage. Variance (loss or shrinkage) comes from miscounting, overpouring, theft or other drivers.

Pars are the minimum a bar wants in stock at all times: historical usage over several months → average weekly usage → × seasonality factor → × target weeks of inventory (a lean 2-week target); update pars at least twice a year.

Inventory counting: estimate partial bottles in tenths (half full = 0.5); always count in the same direction; front bar, back bar, walk-in, storage; arrange the sheet the way bottles are set out; count while the bar is closed; consistent periods (weekly, bi-weekly, monthly); record spillage and breakage; record received stock from invoices.
Inventory tracking is continuous; use one unit of measurement consistently.

2025 standards, mise en place: beverage lists are clean, accurate, up to date and easy to read; glasses spotless and odor-free, polished with linen and steam; trays, ice buckets, stands and decanters clean and ready; tools organized; side stations hold ice buckets and decanters to keep service temperatures. Coravin systems named: Timeless, Pivot, Sparkling; tasks: pouring, recharging, cleaning, replacing gas canisters, changing the needle.

Example feedback: Beverage Assessment means tasting and assessing all beverage alcohol for quality level, production methods, probable pricing, stylistic differences and suitability to program theme. Beverage ID means identifying classic, straightforward types not suitable for the Tasting: spirits, fortified, aromatized and sparkling wines, aperitifs and digestifs.

Wine list design: show vintages, a consistent place of origin and prices; distinguish producer from wine name; readable fonts; don't crowd pages; no background images; hierarchical groups that are understandable and consistent (country, grape or style); navigation cues such as page numbers and section titles.
Core list: Sancerre / Pouilly-Fumé are Loire Valley Sauvignon Blanc.

Storage: constant temperature, 50-60°F / 10-15°C ideal for long term; organized and accessible; away from odors and pests; cork-finished table wines on their side; spirits and fortified standing up; avoid light, vibration, damp, upright storage over a few weeks, heat and temperature swings. Older wines: ask about provenance and storage; inspect for label damage, leakage and ullage.

Preparation: Business of the Sommelier exercises should include staff training: what would their quiz be, how would you teach them? Create a mechanics grid for sparkling and decanting and check it in mock sessions with others or self-recorded; ask why each standard exists; taste all beverages.

Tasting preparation: determine what a list with a certain COGS goal might charge for the wine; how you would train staff to describe the wine in one sentence; how you would serve it and what you'd pair with it.

Introductory: course and exam taken together, in person and online; introduces the deductive tasting method, service standards and a base for theory. Certified: one-day, in-person program after passing Introductory; tests deductive tasting, wine and beverage theory, and tableside service and salesmanship.

unverified: All worked numbers ($20 bottle, $2.40 cocktail, $4.80 flight, $6,000 inventory, 30-bottle par and so on) and the 20% and 25% target cost percentages are our own examples, not Court figures or industry standards.
Variance sign: BevSpot uses cost of product sold minus usage (negative = loss); some other tools reverse it. This chapter uses BevSpot's convention.
'Pour cost' is defined differently across sources (per drink: cost ÷ price; per period: usage ÷ sales). This chapter avoids a single definition and uses cost per ounce and cost % instead.
The Court lists 'audits' without defining them; the audit taught here is the BevSpot variance check.
BevSpot gives two par methods: usage × season × weeks (pars article) and (weekly usage + safety stock) ÷ deliveries per week (Inventory 101). Only the first is taught.
Backbar uses 25.4 oz for a 750 ml bottle; the Court's formulas use 25 oz. This chapter uses 25.
Target cost and markup ranges vary widely between sources (e.g. Provi's 18-20% bar pour cost and 200-300% wine markup); none is stated as a standard.
Toast's wine-pricing and bar-inventory articles could not be loaded (blocked); they are not used.

read.where: From Level 2: cost %, list price and the glass formula. Advanced adds **cocktails** and **flights**, all inside one **50-minute** written exam with a **calculator** and **no negative points**. Every number below is our own example.

stops.name: A bottle
stops.text: Bottle cost ÷ **target cost %** = list price. Example: a $20 bottle at a 25% target lists at **$80**. Starting from a case: case cost ÷ bottles = bottle cost.

stops.name: A cocktail
stops.text: Each pour: **container cost ÷ ounces**, × ounces used. Example: gin from a $25 bottle is $1.00/oz, so 2 oz = $2.00; 1 oz of vermouth from a $10 bottle = $0.40. Total **$2.40**; at a 20% target the price is **$12**.

stops.name: A flight
stops.text: Same method. Example: 2 oz each from $15, $20 and $25 bottles costs $1.20 + $1.60 + $2.00 = **$4.80**; at a 25% target that's **$19.20**.

stops.name: An event
stops.text: Bottles needed = (guests × ounces each) ÷ 25. A **quarter barrel** keg is **992 oz**. Example: 90 pints × 16 oz = 1,440 oz, so order **2 kegs**.

read.mixup: **Cost %** is cost ÷ price: $20 ÷ $80 = 25%. **Markup** is (price - cost) ÷ cost: $60 ÷ $20 = 300%.

read.where: The exam asks you to **read and evaluate inventory sheets**, and the Court lists **audits** and **inventory management** among the skills. From Level 2: COGS = beginning + purchases - ending. At Advanced you compare that **usage** with what the register says you sold.

stops.name: Count it right
stops.text: Count with the bar **closed**, in the **same direction** every time, front bar to storage. Open bottles in **tenths** (half full = 0.5). Keep the sheet in shelf order and log spills and broken bottles.

stops.name: Usage
stops.text: **Beginning + purchases - ending**. Example: $6,000 + $2,000 - $5,500 = **$2,500** used this week.

stops.name: Cost of product sold
stops.text: Pour cost × pours sold, from the POS **product mix**. Example: the week's sales add up to **$2,300** of product.

stops.name: Variance
stops.text: **Sold - used** = -$200. Divide by usage: **-8%**. A negative variance points to **miscounts, overpouring or theft**.

stops.name: Turnover
stops.text: **COGS ÷ average inventory value**. Days in the period ÷ turnover = **days in inventory**. Example: $6,000 ÷ $12,000 = 0.5, so a 30-day month holds 60 days of stock.

read.mixup: **Usage** is what left the shelf. **Cost of product sold** is what the register says you sold. Variance is the gap between them.

read.stopsTitle: Four ways to look at a list

stops.name: Content
stops.text: Choose for the theme, style and **price range**, and know each wine's value in its category. Taste everything you list and know why it's there.

stops.name: Design
stops.text: A clear **hierarchy** (country, grape or style, subdivided the same way), producer set apart from wine name, readable type, white space, no background images, section titles and page numbers.

stops.name: Every entry
stops.text: A **vintage**, a consistent **place of origin** and a **price**. The 2025 standards add that a list must be **clean, accurate and up to date**.

stops.name: Correcting
stops.text: Check spelling, **region and category**, grape and style, vintage, and **price against your formula**. Example: a Sancerre filed under Burgundy moves to the Loire.

read.mixup: **Beverage assessment** judges a drink's quality, style, price and fit. **Beverage ID** names a classic type: a spirit, a fortified or aromatized wine, a sparkling wine.

stops.name: Pars
stops.text: Take several months of **usage**, find the weekly average, adjust for the **season**, multiply by the **weeks of stock** you want. Example: 10 a week × 1.5 × 2 weeks = **30 bottles**.

stops.name: Receiving
stops.text: Record each delivery from its **invoice** so purchases match your counts. Restock **first in, first out**.

stops.name: The cellar
stops.text: A constant **50-60°F (10-15°C)**, away from light, vibration, damp, heat and odors, organized so a bottle is easy to find. Corked wines lie down; **spirits and fortified wines** stand.

stops.name: Equipment
stops.text: Glasses spotless and odor-free; decanters, ice buckets and stands clean and ready at the **side station**; every **Coravin** system cleaned, gassed and fitted with a working needle.

read.mixup: A **par** is the stock you want on hand. **Usage** is what you went through. Pars are built from usage.
